hints: Think about which refinery process breaks long chain alkanes into smaller alkanes plus alkenes, and whether it uses heat alone or heat with a solid.
walkthrough:
Spot the process from the products**
When you see long chain hydrocarbons being turned into smaller alkanes and alkenes, you are looking at cracking. Thermal cracking uses heat alone, but catalytic cracking uses heat with a solid catalyst to work at a lower temperature.

Recall the cracking catalyst**
The standard catalyst for catalytic cracking in AS Chemistry is aluminium oxide, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$. So the compound heated with the long chains is $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.

hints: Start from what leaves the exhaust unburned when petrol does not combust completely, and what forms from $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ at the very high engine temperature.
Think about what those two types of primary pollutants do together in sunlight to make a secondary hazy pollutant.
walkthrough:
Picture what happens inside the engine**
In an internal combustion engine the temperature is extremely high. Petrol does not always burn completely, so some unburned hydrocarbons escape in the exhaust. At the same time, $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ from the air react together to form oxides of nitrogen, mainly $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$.

Link the pollutants to smog in sunlight**
Once in the air, those unburned hydrocarbons react with $\text{NO}$ / $\text{NO}_2$ in the presence of sunlight. This photochemical reaction produces peroxyacetyl nitrate, called PAN, which is a key harmful component of photochemical smog.
Final answer: Unburned hydrocarbons react with $\text{NO}$ / $\text{NO}_2$ to produce PAN, a component of photochemical smog.

hints: Look at the change $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ and decide what type of addition this is and which metal surface is normally used to adsorb the alkene and hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Recognise hydrogenation of an alkene**
$\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ is an alkene and $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ is an alkane. Adding $\text{H}_2$ across the $\text{C=C}$ double bond is hydrogenation, which needs a heterogeneous metal catalyst to adsorb both reactants.

Name the standard metal**
The usual AS example is nickel, $\text{Ni}$, with heat. Platinum, $\text{Pt}$, is also accepted for this addition.

hints: Focus on the word minimum and on what a collision must achieve for bonds to break and new bonds to form, rather than just particles hitting each other.
walkthrough:
Think in terms of collisions**
For a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy to break existing bonds and reach the transition state. Most collisions are just bounces with too little energy.

State the threshold clearly**
Activation energy, $E_A$, is that threshold. It is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for the collision to be effective and lead to reaction.
Final answer: Minimum energy required for a collision to be effective / for reaction to occur.

hints: Picture where $E_A$ sits on the energy axis of Fig. 3.1 and how a catalyst moves that line while leaving the shape and total area of the distribution unchanged.
Connect the size of the area to the right of $E_A$ to the proportion of molecules able to react and to the rate.
walkthrough:
See what the catalyst does to $E_A$**
A catalyst does not change the energies of the molecules, so the Boltzmann curve in Fig. 3.1 stays exactly the same shape. What changes is the activation energy marker. The catalyst gives a new route with a lower $E_A$, so imagine the $E_A$ line shifting to the left to lower energy.

Read the area beyond $E_A$**
Only molecules with energy $\geqslant E_A$ can react, and that is the area under the curve to the right of the $E_A$ line. With the line moved left, that area is much larger. That means a much greater proportion of molecules now have energy equal to or greater than $E_A$.

Link to rate through successful collisions**
Because more molecules can react on collision, the frequency of successful, effective collisions per unit time is higher. More successful collisions means a faster rate of reaction.

Final answer: Catalyst provides an alternative route of lower $E_A$. Area under the Boltzmann curve with energy $\geqslant E_A$ is larger, so a greater proportion of molecules have sufficient energy to react. Frequency of successful collisions increases, so rate increases.
